title: The Kind of Weird You Want to Be
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart takes a comment one of Jim Burke's students made — "it's so weird, Mr. Burke talks about reading and all this stuff like it actually matters" — and argues that this specific kind of weirdness is exactly what American education needs more of. He frames most students' default orientation toward school as utilitarian ("What's in this for me?"), a cultural water they swim in, and argues that a teacher who visibly loves their subject for its own sake models a countercultural alternative. Citing Stanford researcher Bill Damon's finding that many graduates lack a strong sense of purpose, Stuart suggests a simple intervention: tell students why you became a teacher. He closes with three concrete tips — believe in your subject's inherent value, say so explicitly ("mini-sermons"), and get genuinely great at the craft of teaching — tying novelty itself to the Value belief via his "Rainbow of Why" framework.
points: Stuart reframes a student's "that's weird" comment as evidence of a teacher successfully modeling a counterculture to educational utilitarianism, rather than as a compliment to shrug off.
Bill Damon's research-backed recommendation — spend five minutes a year telling students why you became a teacher — offers a low-cost, high-leverage way to make purpose visible to students.
Novelty itself is framed as a legitimate path to student Value (via the "Rainbow of Why"), meaning a teacher's genuine idiosyncratic passion is pedagogically useful, not just charming.
Stuart pairs believing in your subject's value with a mandate to actually say so out loud ("mini-sermons"), arguing private conviction alone doesn't transmit to students.
quotes: It's so weird. Mr. Burke talks about reading and all this stuff like it actually matters. This specific kind of weird, I'll argue, is exactly what we need 1,000,000% more of in American education.

In short, we're a nation of educational utilitarians. This is the predominant culture. And so it should never surprise us when our students come to us demanding to know "when they'll ever use this," how this relates to their desired college or career, or how this connects to the "real world.
What Burke's student noticed, however, is that Burke embodied a counterculture — one in which reading was good because reading was good.

Stanford's Bill Damon spent his career researching a troubling reality: many US high school graduates lack a strong sense of purpose. When asked at the end of his career what he wished all teachers would do to help with this, he gave a simple answer: take at least five minutes per school year to share with your students why you chose to become a teacher.

To be truly weird in your teaching approach, you must wholeheartedly believe in the Value of what you teach. Just as Jim Burke immersed himself in literature and embraced its profound questions, you and I must work at cultivating a deep conviction about the significance of what we teach.
We cannot emanate what we do not have. We cannot give what we don't possess.
Sadly, my last tip points to a hard truth about teaching today: many of the greats have left us. Some have retired. Some have changed careers.
